grammar[1].blocks[0].blocks[1].text: Ich wohne *seit* drei Jahren in Berlin — I still live there, so German uses the present, not the past. Seit *Montag* bin ich krank.

grammar[1].fact: Zeppelins were invented on Lake Constance, in Friedrichshafen, in 1900. You can still fly in one over the lake, which is a calm way to see all three countries and no border at all.

opener.caption: Die Fähre von Konstanz nach Meersburg. Sie fährt zu jeder Tageszeit.
reading.intro: Maya and Lena are cycling around Lake Constance. Lena has a plan, a map and a pump. Maya has a very cheap phone contract, and she is about to learn what that means on this lake.
reading.photos[0].caption: Eine Fähre auf dem Bodensee: In einer Stunde ist man in der Schweiz.
reading.photos[1].caption: An der Grenze am Bodensee: Hier sieht man fast nichts davon.
reading.en: Lena: Now we’ll cycle to the ferry. From Konstanz to Meersburg. Then we’ll stay at my aunt’s. · Maya: I’ve been riding on a broken tyre for an hour. · Lena: We’ll fix it after the ferry. I’ll take the pump out of my rucksack. · Maya’s phone goes "ping". · Maya: Lena! It says here: Welcome to Switzerland! · Lena: That’s normal. Switzerland is opposite the harbour. · Ping. · Maya: Now: Welcome to Austria! · Lena: Also normal. The lake belongs to everyone. Come over here, we’re at the ferry. · Ping. · Maya: Lena! A message from my phone company. Internet in Switzerland costs twelve euros. Per minute! · Lena: How long were you online? · Maya: For an hour. I was looking for the way with the map. Your way, your map, my money. · Lena: After the ferry we’ll be in Germany. Then you won’t pay any more. · Ping. Welcome to Germany! And then, on the bike: psssst. The second tyre.
reading.fact: The border on Lake Constance has never been fully agreed. Germany, Austria and Switzerland each read the map their own way, and Switzerland’s view is that the line runs through the middle. It has worked fine for centuries with nobody really deciding.

document.intro: A real sign at a small car ferry, this one on the Elbe. *Weiterfahrt* means driving on, *Aufforderung* means being told to, and *das Fährpersonal* are the people working on the ferry.
document.fact: Germany still has many small river ferries, and some of them run with no engine at all: the river pushes them along a cable. On the Elbe a crossing costs a euro or two, and you pay the man at the rail.
